utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam Registrar. And good afternoon, everybody. Could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. All the accused are here, for the record. From the Defence teams I notice the absence of Mr. Haynes, Mr. Josse, Mr. Petrusic; is that correct? I'm not seeing him. Yes. Madam Nikolic and Mr. Ostojic. Prosecution I notice same composition as yesterday. So yesterday, before we rose, I told you we'll have one hour, and I encouraged you to discuss how you were going to share the time. If perhaps one of you could come back to us and tell us what you have agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. If I'm correct, I think that the Borovcanin team would like 25 to 30 minutes and Mr. Meek, and I will split up what's the rest, 50/50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And what about responses and replies and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, I'll be going last so I'll fit mine in. I think I don't know how they want to divide theirs up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May I start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Your Honours, the first question to which I wish to address myself in presenting my argumentation is the question of voluntariness. According to the position of Mr. Borovcanin's Defence team, voluntariness is a multi-facetted category which can be considered from a number of aspects. The first aspect of voluntariness in the strict sense of the word would refer to whether compulsion, coercive force, or a series threat was applied in respect of Mr. Borovcanin in order for him to grant this interview and whether such coercion or threats was applied during the actual giving of the interview. The Defence of Mr. Borovcanin answers this question with a no, it was not the case. In the system from which I come, the second aspect of voluntariness is called the defective consent, and this is equally as important for evaluating the admissibility of a specific exhibit. In the specific case, the Defence should like to stress that this Trial Chamber should establish whether, when giving his interview, Mr. Borovcanin was aware of his position in the proceedings in which he was taking part and whether he was fully cognizant of all his rights which emanate from his position. The onus probandi to the effect that the interviews of Mr. Borovcanin were given in all respects in accordance with valid and generally accepted rules and principles is on the Prosecutor, and to that effect, the Prosecutor has brought the witness Alistair Graham, in the view of the Defence, it was precisely the testimony of this witness that confirmed our position that Mr. Borovcanin from the beginning of his talk with representatives of the OTP was not aware of his legal position in the proceedings, nor had he been regularly and completely advised of the rights in which he has on the basis of his status. In such a situation the fact that Mr. Borovcanin is -- was proceeding under a misconception in respect of his status, and the rights that he had, are the basis for these interviews and the accompanying documents not to be admitted into the file of this case. The notion of the accused is defined under Rule 2 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the Tribunal, and it says that the accused is a person in respect of which the Prosecutor has reliable information which indicate the possibility of that person having committed a criminal offence for which this International Tribunal has jurisdiction. Under Rule 42 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, this rule actually defines the rights of the accused during investigation and that is the point of departure from which we must start when we analyse this question; namely, whether at the time of giving his statement, Mr. Borovcanin was giving his statement, all the conditions from this rule were indeed fulfilled in order to make it possible to adopt a decision on the admissibility of that interview. Mr. Borovcanin even received an invitation to meet with representatives of the OTP in order to give a statement. In the invitation, it was stated in the summons that he had the status of an accused, and this is not contested by the Defence. However, the summons did not indicate the actual rights which Mr. Borovcanin has as an accused, such as the right to refrain from giving a statement, the right to legal assistance, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just want to make sure that interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It's a mistake in transcript [overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not a status of an accused but is, I suppose you said a status of a suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Suspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Correct. Thank you. Go ahead. I just wanted to ask the interpreter who is translating to us in English whether Mr. Lazarevic is going too fast for her.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No, no, it's all right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I provided written text to the interpreters, so this is why it's going smoothly. [Interpretation] Already during the first interview conducted by the investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor, Mr. Graham, informed Ljubomir Borovcanin that he, Mr. Borovcanin, could be or may be a suspect for crimes or criminal acts envisaged by the Statute of the Tribunal. This very formulation, "May be a suspect" can be interpreted in only one way. "You are not a suspect but you could become one." Is there any other reason why Mr. Borovcanin could draw any other conclusion than the one I just suggested? Mr. Borovcanin is not a lawyer, his legal adviser was not present at that time, and his understanding of the status he had in the proceedings could only be that of a layman. Mr. Borovcanin was certainly labouring under a legal misconception concerning his status; namely, from the interview it is clear that Borovcanin was told not only at the beginning but several times during the interview that he was a possible suspect. A potential suspect. That concept does not exist either in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the Tribunal, nor in the relevant legislation of other jurisdictions. In an investigation, a person can be a suspect or a witness, but they cannot be a potential suspect. To compound this confusion and misconception, although Mr. Borovcanin received the interpretation at one point that he was a suspect, the following cautions in the course of the interview again sounded as "possible suspect". Mr. Graham testified that during the interview he used and relied on a standardised aide-memoire when he had to caution Mr. Borovcanin and advise him of his rights. Nevertheless, every caution was given or formulated differently or was interpreted differently to Mr. Borovcanin. Mr. Graham did say to Mr. Borovcanin that his statement could be used against Mr. Borovcanin personally in trial proceedings. However, due to inadequate interpretation, Mr. Borovcanin was not actually advised of that. Thus, he was not informed that the statement he was giving may be used against him. The Defence believed -- believes that this caution is of special importance when it concerns the rights of a suspect. Such a person when deciding whether to grant an interview or not must be clearly advised of their status when giving the statement. To be more precise, out of the six cautions given to Mr. Borovcanin in the course of two interviews concerning his own rights during the process, on four occasions he did not receive the interpretation that what he was saying can be used, "against him." Which again indubitably points to the fact that Ljubomir Borovcanin could be confused about his status. The lack of adequate caution is perhaps an error in translation, although two interpreters made the same mistake, which may lead this Trial Chamber to believe that these words might be superfluous in B/C/S. This is undoubtedly an error on the interpreters part because the second interview does include the words "against you" at one point. And that really is an error because in the legal system from which Mr. Borovcanin comes, an important element of the caution given to the person granting the statement is precisely the phrase that "the statement may be used against that person". Even if, for argument's sake, we were to assume that the words "against you" do not have to be said in B/C/S, the role of the interpreter is not to interpret the rules of any legal system but to interpret as accurately as possible what is being said to the best of their ability. Therefore, the error that occurred as a result of inadequate interpretation must not and should not have negative consequences on Mr. Borovcanin or his fundamental rights to a fair trial, his right to defend himself by silence and the right not to incriminate himself. This situation should be viewed from the position that at that time Mr. Borovcanin did not know or at least was not sure that the statement he was giving may be used in proceedings against him personally. Mr. Borovcanin was cautioned that he did not have to answer the questions, but at no time was it clearly stated to him that he did not have to speak to the Office of the Prosecutor at all and that that right includes that at any point he was free to stop and leave the interview. The Defence holds the opinion that this right also should have been clearly and unequivocally stated to Mr. Borovcanin so that he could consciously and of his free will decide whether to exercise that right or not. There was no time in any of the interviews when Mr. Borovcanin was clearly told of which crimes he was suspected or which form of responsibility or liability envisaged by the Statute of the Tribunal is involved. The Office of the Prosecutor limited itself to the formulation, "Acts in the jurisdiction of the Tribunal." If that were to happen in any criminal trial, in any legal system, that would be reduced to the following: "You may be suspected of some crime that is envisaged by the Criminal Code of this country." The Defence of Mr. Borovcanin believes that this caution addressed to Mr. Borovcanin was at least insufficient,. And based on such a caution, he was not able to know whether the answers he was giving were incriminating him or not. There is no evidence that Mr. Borovcanin was aware of all the criminal acts envisaged by the Statute of the Tribunal. Mr. Graham also confirmed that the Office of the Prosecutor did not know either whether Mr. Borovcanin or his legal adviser were even aware of the Statute and the rules of the Tribunal. At this moment, I can only say with certainty that at the time he was giving the statement, neither Mr. Borovcanin nor his counsel were really aware of that. Furthermore, the Statute of the ICTY covers a large number of acts of varying gravity, varying descriptions, and it can certainly not be assumed that Mr. Borovcanin could have been aware of all of them. Similarly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm very sorry to object. I understand this is argument. However, and I haven't been but here I think I have to object to the line at this moment, at line 22 page 7, "I can only say with certainty that at the time he was giving the statement neither Mr. Borovcanin nor his counsel were really aware of that." That's the -- that's the kind of evidence where evidence must be called when an assertion that direct is made. There is -- my friend I think is perfectly clear to say that's a rational conclusion that one could draw from the interview, but I'm sorry I'll sit down. I just don't think he should make direct statements of facts which are not supported in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, do you wish to respond to that, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I agree with Mr. Nicholls and I apologise. It was certainly not my intention to testify, but this is -- I was just commenting on what we heard from Mr. Graham and that was it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Similarly, Mr. Borovcanin could not have known that he could also be suspected of command responsibility and that speaking of the activities of others he could incriminate himself as well. Finally, the Defence of Mr. Borovcanin wishes to emphasise that Mr. Borovcanin, as we heard from Mr. Graham, is not a lawyer, and his ability to understand such cautions or lack of them should be viewed through the prism of the fact that his legal counsel was not present at the time. Regards to the question of cautioning or advisement, the Defence team of Mr. Borovcanin would like to quote the appropriate provisions of the law and criminal procedure of some of the states of the former Yugoslavia in order to acquaint the Trial Chamber with the standard which in this respect should be satisfied in our opinion. The law and criminal procedure of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Article 78, para 2, says, "At the beginning of the questioning, the suspect shall be informed of which criminal offence -- with which criminal offence he's been charged and the grounds of suspicion against him." Similarly to this, Article 5 of the law on criminal procedure of the Republic of Serbia which incidentally equalises the concept of accused and suspect envisages the following: "Prior to his first hearing, the accused shall be warned that everything that he states can be used as proof against him." In paragraph 2, it states that already at the first hearing, the accused must be informed of the offence that he's being charged with and on the evidence on which the charges are grounded; and lastly, I shall quote Article 186 of the law on criminal procedure of the Republic of Croatia which in its relevant part, which is item 5, envisages that in collecting information, the police authorities, the law enforcement, shall inform and caution the accused in keeping with the provisions of Article 2372 of this law. He shall be informed of the charges against him, and the basic grounds of suspicion against him and also cautioned that he does not have to present his defence nor to respond to any questions. I should just like to state that I only quote the relevant parts of these articles. The provisions which I have just quoted clearly show the standard which has been adopted by the states whose legislation I have just quoted from, in respect of the necessary informing of suspects. It is equally clear that these cautions go beyond what the investigator, Mr. Graham, advised Mr. Borovcanin on the occasion of the giving of his statement. This standard is very clear. Before deciding whether to give a statement or not, the suspect must be informed of the actual charges against him and the factual basis from which emanates the grounded suspicion that he had committed that offence. Obviously, when Mr. Borovcanin was giving his statement to the OTP, this standard had not been satisfied. The question which arises is which standard in respect of this legal issue shall be adopted by this Trial Chamber. The Defence allows for the possibility that this question may be addressed in different ways in different legal systems, as well as that this Tribunal, as an International Tribunal, dispenses justice according to different rules in respect of each individual legislation. However, precisely because of the fact that this is an International Tribunal and given the historic role which this Court has in creating the jurisprudence of international criminal law, Mr. Borovcanin's Defence team suggests that in respect of this question, the Trial Chamber should be guided by the highest possible standards in the very least those which are envisaged in the legislations which I have just quoted. In particular, as this is the International Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia, it is the view of the Defence that the Trial Chamber should in any case pay due attention to also the legislations of the countries of that former Yugoslavia. I shall now move on to the subject of the legal representation of Mr. Borovcanin during the giving of the interview. It has already been mentioned that according to the rules of the legal system from which Mr. Borovcanin and his Defence team hail, grave criminal offences entail the principle of necessary defence or more precisely to put it, an accused or suspected person for such criminal offences must have a legal representative who has to be present at each and every moment during the granting of the suspect's statement. It is a fact that Mr. Borovcanin's lawyer did not attend the first part of his interview on the 20th of February 2002. It is equally a fact that Mr. Borovcanin actually agreed to that. However, Mr. Borovcanin's consent for the interview to continue in the absence of Defence counsel should actually be viewed through the prism of the arguments which I have already adduced, namely: Would Mr. Borovcanin have indeed consented for that interview to be conducted without a legal representative had he clearly known that his was the status of a suspect, would he have consented had he clearly and unequivocally known that what he was saying could be used against him personally, and would he have consented had he known that he was a suspect for the criminal offence of genocide and conspiracy to commit genocide? In other words, the question is would Mr. Borovcanin have at all talked to the Office of the Prosecutor and in particular without the presence of legal counsel? As regards the role which a legal representative should have, the Defence should like to stress the following: In keeping with Article 18.3 of the Tribunal's statute and Rule 42 of the rules of procedure, the suspect is entitled to be assisted by a lawyer of his own choice meaning that it is the duty of legal counsel to assist the person being represented. That implies an active role in the proceedings, whether it is in the pre-trial stage or in the actual trial stage. Such an interpretation and such a perception of the right of the suspect to lawyers has also been accepted in the practice of this Tribunal as well, and I should like to invoke the decisions in the Blagojevic-Jokic case of 18 September 2003, paragraph 25. Mr. Borovcanin's defence contends that apart from being merely present for a certain -- during a certain part of this interview, the legal representatives of Mr. Borovcanin in no way actually assisted Mr. Borovcanin, nor did they effectively protect his rights. There is no dispute about the question that it was with Mr. Borovcanin's consent that the interview of the 20th of February 2002 started and was conducted for a full three hours without the presence of a legal representative. Even at the point when his legal counsel, Mr. Zoran Bubic, actually joined the interview, that transpired without any concrete input on his part. He neither said anything, nor did he suggest anything, nor did he in any way whatsoever extend any legal assistance to his client. He, in fact, did not even see fit to check what had been said in his absence, nor whether he, as the designated Defence counsel, agreed for the interview to proceed from the point at which he had joined it or whether it should start over from the beginning. He also failed to interview a single time -- to -- sorry, intervene a single time in situations when it was required to clarify the status and the extent of the rights that Mr. Borovcanin had during the interview. The formal presence of Mr. Borovcanin's legal counsel during a part of the interview cannot be justification for failure to perform the function entrusted to him, which is to assist his client. He simply did not do that, whereby Mr. Borovcanin was deprived of the effective -- of effective legal representation. When he was giving the second interview, Mr. Goran Bubic, another, a new legal representative, appeared also and again with the consent of Mr. Borovcanin. Not even this second lawyer participated in any way whatsoever in extending legal assistance to his client. Mr. Bubic literally did not say a single word that would concern his -- that would amount to his extending legal assistance to his client. Apart from that, the question of the continuity of defence also arises because we do not know whether the first lawyer actually informed the second lawyer on what had happened during the first interview. It is in the view of the position of -- it is in the position of the Defence team of Mr. Borovcanin that also grounds for which the interview and the attending documentation should not be admitted into the case file. Mr. Borovcanin's Defence team would like to stress another question which it deems to be of importance for the adoption of a proper decision in this legal matter. At the end of the interview, Mr. Borovcanin was given the possibility to ask to change or further clarify some of the things that he had said during the interview and that all he needed to do that was to inform the OTP accordingly. The interviews with Mr. Borovcanin lasted for about 15 hours, and it is clear to any sensible person that there does not exist a person that has such a command -- such concentration that he could precisely remember any question and answer given during an interview that was conducted for 15 hours, and especially not the person who is giving a statement, without listening to the tapes. That certainly would not be possible in the absence of such an aid. There was not a single valid reason for Mr. Borovcanin not to be provided the tapes from the interview -- of the interview within a period of a couple of days. However, that was not done. It is quite clear from yesterday's and today's testimony that at the beginning of the second interview, Mr. Borovcanin did not have the audio tapes from the previous hearing, nor had any of his lawyers received these tapes. On the contrary, he was given the right to change or supplement something in his interview, but de facto that right was limited because he hadn't got the tapes in a timely fashion. And to wrap up, it is the position of the Defence of Mr. Borovcanin that the interviews were obtained in a way which did not fully abide by the basic rights of Mr. Borovcanin and that accordingly no adverse consequence vis-a-vis Mr. Borovcanin may arise out of them. Hence, the Defence should like to stress that admission of the interview of Mr. Borovcanin into the case file would not be in the interests of justice, nor would it be in conformity with the principle of a fair trial, and it proposes that this Trial Chamber adopt a decision dismissing the Prosecutor's motion for the interview, and the accompanying documents to be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Lazarevic. Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'll try to keep this as short as possible. First off, and Mr. Lazarevic has pointed this out and that's Rule 42, which states that a suspect who is to be questioned by the Prosecutor shall have the following rights. And the Prosecutor shall inform the suspect prior to questioning. This is mandatory, not discretionary, and the reason and the purpose for such warnings is to neutralise the distinct psychological disadvantage that suspects are under when they are dealing with law enforcement officers or the Office of the Prosecutor in this case. Under the voluntariness test, the Prosecution must prove, I submit, that they read specific warnings and obtained an intelligent waiver. I submit, Your Honours, that they cannot show this in this case. An interrogation is inherently -- inherently involves persuasion and pressure. The ultimate goal of any interrogation is to obtain a confession or at least an admission. Anything -- anything that would implicate the suspect in criminal behaviour. It can safely be assumed that nobody, none of us, would voluntarily implicate ourselves to the police but interrogation such as we have here necessarily involves persuading or convincing a person that it would be in their best interest to do so. Interrogation, in fact, is a changing of a person's mind so that they want to tell the police or law enforcement everything they did, therefore helping to convict themselves. The Prosecution in this case has talked a lot in the last week or so to Your Honours about the only issue is voluntariness: Was the statement given voluntarily? I respectfully submit that that is only the second prong of the analysis that Your Honours are going to have to delve into. I submit that the Prosecution has the burden to prove first that the suspect, Mr. Borovcanin, knowingly, intelligently and voluntarily waived his rights and thereafter, that he, Mr. Borovcanin, voluntarily gave his statement. This burden is a heavy burden and it is never placed on the Defence. Again, I believe that the Prosecution wants Your Honours to focus on was the statements -- were the statements voluntarily given? Well, no one claims that anyone held a gun to his head. However, the point being that the Prosecution has to prove that Mr. Borovcanin, who what is a suspect at the time, who was served with a summons to appear as a suspect under Rule 42, that he knowingly and intelligently waived the rights under Rule 42. The requirement, the simple requirement, that the waiver of these rights be knowing and intelligent, ensures that a defendant or an accused or a suspect in this case is aware of these rights, further the requirement that a waiver be voluntary protects the trustworthiness of the statement by ensuring that the suspect was not coerced into confessing or giving statements against himself falsely. Further, Your Honours, once a suspect has made an incriminating statement, it is unlikely that in that event that he would feel free to retract those statements or refuse to speak further to the person whom he had just given the statements after he had been issued the warnings. This is what I would call, Your Honour, and has been called, letting the cat out of the bag by giving the statement and no matter what the inducement, the person who has given it is never thereafter really free of the psychological and practical disadvantages of having given that statement in the first place. I submit, Your Honours, that the Office of the Prosecutor has not come close to showing and meeting their burden that this statement should be admitted against Mr. Borovcanin based on the fact that it was voluntary. They cannot show, Your Honours, that there was a knowing, intelligent, and voluntary waiver of the rights due to the fact that you heard yesterday and due to the fact that Mr. Lazarevic just spoke about. He was told he was a possible suspect. He was told because of a bad interpretation that "anything would be used against him" rather than just "used in court." I submit, Your Honour, that the OTP by using this document to read these rights and tell Mr. Borovcanin that he was a possible suspect was nothing less than subterfuge. It was nothing less than a ruse, a trick, a device, to obtain an advantage over him to get him to give the statement. Another way you could put it, Your Honours, is that, and I submit, that because of the way the rights were read to him, that it was also the statement was produced based on fraud and inducement; that the OTP used a deceitful warning as a trick to cause him to act to his disadvantage. I submit, Your Honours, that Rule 42 has been violated, they cannot show and they have not shown any -- under any burden, a preponderance of the evidence, by clear and convincing evidence, or beyond a reasonable doubt, that Mr. Borovcanin voluntarily, knowingly, and intelligently waived the rights afforded him by the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Finally, Your Honours, I just want to say that if any trial is worth conducting, then it's worth conducting fairly. And the courts that apply this principle rigorously become stronger and not weaker. This statement should not be admitted, and we request that you disallow it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Meek. Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you to my friends and Your Honour for the time. I'll try to finish in the 15, 14 minutes that are left. I'll shorten my presentation a little bit. Our position, Your Honours, is that this interview, I think, is entirely admissible. It's probative, it's reliable, all the procedural safeguards required under the statute were fully complied with. It was given voluntarily and knowingly and intelligently by Mr. Borovcanin. The crux, I think we can see, of the issue here is Rule 42 and whether it was complied with. Mr. Lazarevic on behalf of his client has gone through a great deal of explaining what the law is that Mr. Borovcanin would have been familiar with, the law of the former Yugoslavia regarding interrogation and things of that nature. That is entirely irrelevant. First of all, for it to be relevant, it would mean that Mr. Borovcanin, the Professor of law enforcement, would have been aware of that law for it to have affected his thinking. If he was aware of that law, he -- and was able to understand those concepts and compare them while he was being interviewed, he surely would have been able to understand the very simple rights -- reading of the rights which was given to him at his interviews; and more importantly, the case law of this Tribunal makes it clear that the cultural differences defence holds no water whatsoever. I'm talking there primarily to the decision on Zdravko Mucic's motion for the exclusion of evidence, that's the Celebici case, IT-96-21-T, 2nd September 1997, specifically starting at paragraph 59 to 60. There, the Trial Chamber specifically addressing Rule 42 states that the test is an objective test. The question is whether Rule 42 was read out, and it is the -- the test is not whether the person had any familiarity with that from their culture, and the reason for that makes good sense which they refer to; which the rights, as listed -- the exhaustive rights and specific rights in Rule 42 are derived from international norms from the European Convention of Human Rights, the international -- ICCPR, and they are specifically designed to apply to all situations, all people. These rights were designed to be easily understood by people from the Former Yugoslavia when they were put in our statute and to comply with international norms. I urge you to read those paragraphs as well as paragraphs 551 to 553 of the Celebici judgement -- appeals judgement, excuse me, which affirms that. In talking about Rule 42 in paragraph 551, the Appeals Chamber said, "The right is neither ambiguous nor difficult to understand, as long as a suspect is clearly informed of its language, in a language he or she understands, the Prosecution fulfils its obligation. An investigator is not obliged to go further." And I won't because of the time go through it, but in the Halilovic decision, 8 July 2005 for exclusion of the statement of the accused, paragraphs 22 and 23, they make it very clear that what this Tribunal requires under our Statute and our Rules of Procedure, is that "A suspect be informed that he had the right to remain silent and that any statement he may make may be used in evidence," period. There is no requirement that the words, as my friend would like to add, "Be used against you." The investigator in this case was going further than the requirement. I think it was very clear from his testimony that what he was trying to do was to be as fair as possible to Mr. Borovcanin and make sure that he understood those rights. He went beyond the rule. The argument that Mr. Borovcanin should have waited for his counsel to appear or that he was free to leave the room, all of those arguments, I urge you to read how many times the investigator and Mr. McCloskey on pages 1 and 2 of the first interview told Mr. Borovcanin that it was an important matter, and he should wait for his lawyer if he wanted to and that he was under no obligation. And Mr. Borovcanin said, "I want to start." He was read and advised his rights in a very simple fashion which complied to the rules and he said, "I want to start." And again, just to go back to Halilovic, the key here, the key for you, is was he informed that he had the right not to answer any questions and to remain silent? Yes. That's the rule. The rule was complied with. Was he told that anything he said could be used in evidence? Yes. And he was told that many times, both before his lawyer arrived and after his lawyer arrived. I want to comment briefly on the -- very briefly on the attack on the competency of his counsel or the claim that counsel was ineffective. It cannot be that simply because the lawyer did not ask questions or interrupt that that constitutes somehow ineffective assistance of counsel. First of all, when counsel arrived, what the record shows is that there was a two-hour gap, break, specifically for him to consult with his client, and all of the questions, all of the questions posed by Mr. Lazarevic, that he wondered why the lawyer did not ask the investigator could have been answered by Mr. Borovcanin during those two hours, and it's just really raw, gross speculation to try to say that somehow this lawyer listening to the evidence and with his client was ineffective merely because he didn't jump up at certain points. And I think we need to look at the reality of what happened during this interview step by step. Mr. Borovcanin, it's clear from the record, is an educated man, highly educated man. At the time of the interview he had a master's degree, he was a life-long career police officer, he was working as a professor in law enforcement at Banja Luka at the academy, and he was working on a Ph.D. This man was summonsed as a suspect and that summons says that "He is to provide a statement in respect of an investigation into crimes that occurred in and around Srebrenica in 1995." He's also given a safe conduct or Prosecutor's undertaking which said that you will not be arrested at the interview or for five days after the interview or on the way to or from the interview. He retained an attorney prior to the interview at some point after he received the summons. He unambiguously waived his right to have that counsel present more than once at the beginning of the interview. If you look through this interview, most especially in the February interview, at pages 2, 23, 44, 1, 115, and the March interview at pages 1, 115, 50, you'll see that all the rights were complied with. And really what my friends are trying to do is set up an impossible standard, a standard in which no interview would be admissible because what they are attacking is not so much the way their rights were administered in this, but saying that Article 42 is inadequate because it doesn't say "You have to be advised of your status as suspect," it doesn't say that. And because it doesn't say that "Evidence may be used against you," because it doesn't have those extra words, "Against you." Those rules are the same one that is have been used since the beginning of this institution. They were complied with in this case, and it is just simply not complicated, as they would try to have it. I can understand if they had called some evidence that Mr. Borovcanin had some kind of mental impairment, if he had some specific difficulty in understanding very, very plain language like that contained in rules 42 and 43. The interpretation, there have been some mistakes, but we've corrected that in the transcript, and over all, it was very accurate. He received everything he needed to know under the rules, and we've also learned that he speaks English to some degree as well. So, finally, I would say in answer to my friend Mr. Meek, was it knowing? Yes. This is a man working on a Ph.D. hearing very simple rules which are a universal standard that applied to him and applied in the Former Yugoslavia as well as they were a member of those international instruments. Was it intelligently waived? If you read the transcript you'll see that he understood. He says, "Yes, we can continue." He answers the question intelligently. My friend said that at the end of the interview he was told he could contact the Prosecution later. Well, actually, he was referring to page 162, I think, and they are when Mr. Borovcanin is given the opportunity to add or clarify and that's at the second interview, he does so. He says that he makes some comments on the structure. And was there a waiver? Yes. The waivers are express all the way through. The waiver of his right to remain silent, the waiver of his right to counsel. It's completely unambiguous. He understood his rights and he waived them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Nicholls. Do you wish to add anything, Mr. Lazarevic? Or shall we leave it at that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour, since I see that we have a minute left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Two things. It doesn't matter under these circumstances that Mr. Borovcanin was a very educated man. Here is a man who has never been in the shoes of a suspect. He's there in Banja Luka at the United Nations building. He is without his lawyer. He is with an investigator and a senior legal attorney from the OTP; and frankly, Your Honour, we are not trying to set up an impossible standard, and the Prosecution says this a lot. We just would like the Prosecution to abide by the rules, and the rules are that they shall do these and it's not discretionary. So that's all I have to say, Your Honours. I thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think we can safely close the debate on this issue here. We will not be rendering a decision today or tomorrow. I think we need to mull over the whole -- all the submissions that you have made. We do not have any further business to transact until after the recess, and, of course, I told you yesterday we'll meet on the 21st of August, not because we have decided to reject the joinder motion but because hope springs eternal, Mr. McCloskey, but because we are scheduled to sit on that day. So until then, or until we meet again, I wish to take this opportunity and speak on behalf of both Judge Kwon, Judge Stole, and Judge Prost, to thank you for all the work that you have put in the case. I know you have a very hard task, all of you, Prosecution and Defence. It's not an easy case by any means. And it's very demanding on your time and on your energies. You've worked a lot, and the number of motions and the level of your interventions indicate your preparation for the case on a daily basis. We appreciate that. I think a break is what we all need at the moment. So what remains to be said on my part is to wish you a good rest, and to come back, please God, come all back in August when we meet again, and then we can take it up from there. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 21st day of August, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.33 p.m.,
